extracted.intended_audience: students and educated readers of philosophy/natural history/social evolution (general readers of 19th-century scientific-philosophical works)
extracted.subtask_description: A conceptual exposition that defines Evolution as a general law: a process transforming incoherent homogeneity into coherent heterogeneity via integration and dissipation of motion, supplemented by a required advance from the indefinite to the definite. Illustrated across language, the arts, music, literature, science, and social phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution: incoherent homogeneity → coherent heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolution is definable as a change from an incoherent homogeneity to a coherent heterogeneity, accompanying the dissipation of motion and integration of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the author's central, general formula. It should be applied when judging whether a process is 'evolutionary' — i.e., does the whole move from a less-structured, uniform state to a more structured, varied state while integrating matter and dissipating motion? Examples given span geologic, biological, social, linguistic, and artistic change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance from the homogeneous to the heterogeneous by successive differentiations
rubrics_metrics.description: The advance from the homogeneous to the heterogeneous is effected through a process of successive differentiations (the gradual multiplication and specialization of parts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to identify evolutionary change as successive splitting and specialization of functions/parts (e.g., verbs differentiating into active and passive; nouns into abstract and concrete; parts of speech forming auxiliaries, adjectives, adverbs, etc.). The text illustrates this across language, arts, and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-ordinate origin and gradual separation of allied forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Related forms (e.g., rhythm in speech, rhythm in sound, rhythm in motion — poetry, music, dancing) have co‑ordinate origins and subsequently undergo gradual differentiation into separate arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when assessing whether multiple related practices or forms have evolved from a shared root into distinct specialized forms. Examples: ritual chants/dances giving rise to separate poetry, music, and dance; minstrels uniting poet/composer/performer roles that later separate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration/concentration accompanies differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: While the aggregate concentrates (integration of matter, closer approach of parts), the distinct parts also become unlike — i.e., parts differentiate while the whole becomes more coherent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This dual movement (integration of the whole + differentiation of parts) is essential to the author's conception of compound evolution. When evaluating a process, check for both increasing internal cohesion of the aggregate and increasing specialization among its parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution includes increase in definiteness (indefinite → definite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Along with an advance from simplicity to complexity, there is an advance from confusion to order — from undetermined arrangement to determined arrangement; evolution is a change from the indefinite to the definite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supplementary distinction is required to separate true evolution from mere increases in heterogeneity. True evolutionary change should produce well‑defined, regularly positioned, and proportionate parts (e.g., organs, artistic conventions), not merely chaotic or irregular variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: heterogeneity without definiteness is not Evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes that increase heterogeneity but lack definiteness, coherence, or integration (e.g., local disease, putrefaction, social disorder) are not Evolution but steps toward dissolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explicitly contrasts morbid growths, decomposition, rebellions, commercial derangement, etc., as examples where heterogeneity increases but the result lacks the precise, definite, integrated character of evolutionary development. Use these as negative tests: if heterogeneity is irregular, poorly localized, variable in size/form, and internally confused, do not classify it as evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for supplementary distinctions beyond the simple formula
rubrics_metrics.description: The simple formula ('homogeneous → heterogeneous') is imperfect and requires supplementing (notably by the definiteness criterion) to exclude non-evolutionary redistributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying the general formula, practitioners should check additional qualifications (e.g., definiteness, coherence, integration) rather than treating any increase of heterogeneity as evolutionary. The author signals that the generalization must be refined to be exclusive of unrelated phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successive differentiation illustrated in concrete cultural/technical domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete historical series (language: hieroglyphics → hieratic → epistolary → phonetic symbols → alphabetic writing; arts: mural decoration → picture-writing → symbols → alphabets; music: percussive rhythm → lyres with more strings → modes → fugue → harmony → concerted music) exemplify the process of differentiation increasing heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These domain-specific sequences serve as operational examples of how to recognize evolutionary differentiation in practice: look for incremental additions (new instruments, modes, signs), partial innovations (phonetic symbols used alongside ideographs), and eventual multiplication of specialized forms (many musical genres, alphabets, parts of speech). Use these examples to ground abstract assessments.
